title: Ask, don't tell
hook: don't dwell on your own deeds and dangers; others don't enjoy them as you do (Enchiridion 33)
carry: hands the stage to someone else

segments.voice: Yesterday: oaths, laughter, and the plain word. Your line was a word that doesn't need help. Which promise did you keep without swearing? Day three hundred sixty-seven.

Everyone has been on the receiving end of this. Dinner, a long table, and someone is telling the story of their near miss on the highway. Or the marathon. Or the time they told the boss exactly what they thought. It's the third time you've heard it, and it's getting longer. And here's the uncomfortable part: everyone has also been the one telling it. Section thirty-three, still sketching how to behave in company, has a line for exactly this. Today: ask, don't tell.
screen: `DINNER, AND THE NEAR-MISS STORY.` → `THE THIRD TIME YOU'VE HEARD IT.` → `ASK, DON'T TELL.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. In company, Epictetus says, don't keep bringing up your own deeds and your own dangers, often and at length. Second, the reason, and it's disarmingly honest. However pleasant it is for you to recall your dangers, it isn't as pleasant for other people to hear about them. That's it. No grand theory. Just an observation anyone can check at the next dinner party. Our own stories glow for us because we were in them. For everyone else, they're secondhand. Third, the line that comes right after. Avoid playing for laughs, he says. It slides easily into vulgarity, and it tends to lower the respect the people around you have for you. The common thread is the spotlight. Telling your adventures and working the room for a laugh both turn a conversation into a stage with one performer. Fourth, the turn. The handbook doesn't say ask in so many words; that's how this path carries it. But it fits the man Epictetus admired most. Socrates, in Plato's dialogues, is famous for asking questions, so many that it became a method named after him. If you're not telling, you have room to ask. How was your week? What happened next? What was that like for you? A question hands the stage to someone else. It's a small trade: one story fewer told, one more heard all the way to the end.
screen: `DON'T DWELL ON YOUR OWN EXPLOITS.` · `YOUR DANGERS THRILL YOU, NOT THEM.` · `DON'T PLAY FOR LAUGHS.` · `SOCRATES ASKED.` · then, large: `ASK, DON'T TELL.`

segments.voice: Sit back, and breathe. Think of someone you'll talk with today: a coworker, a friend, a parent, a child, the person at the counter. Picture the moment you'd usually start telling them your news. Now picture asking them a question instead, and actually waiting for the answer. Which question? How are you, really. What's been the best part of your week. What are you working on. Choose one and keep it ready. The bell holds the time.
Ask. Enchiridion thirty-three: don't keep telling your own deeds and dangers. Others don't enjoy them as much as you do. Leave room to ask. Today's word.
Your line: hands the stage to someone else. In one conversation today, ask more and tell less. Ask a real question, and let the answer have the floor. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes set themselves a simple conversational habit: fewer stories about their own exploits and more questions about the other person.

fork.setup: a friend mentions a scary drive home last night. you had a scarier one last year. what fits Epictetus' advice?
options: tell yours. it's a better story.

fork.reveal: he says not to dwell on your own dangers; others don't enjoy them as you do. asking keeps the stage where it belongs.

original.note: Greek: danger. Enchiridion 33 warns against dwelling on your own.

trapdoor: what it means: even honest stories of your deeds and dangers please you more than your listeners, so tell fewer and ask more.
what a scholar hears: the rule's reason is plain observation, not doctrine, and it sits beside a warning against playing for laughs.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): removed an unsourced superlative in the hook ('the most quietly funny sentence in the whole handbook') and an unsupported claim about what people remember at the end of the teach.

Enchiridion 33 paraphrased: avoid mentioning frequently and at length your own acts and dangers, because it is not as pleasant for others to hear as for you to mention them; avoid raising laughter, which slips into vulgarity and lessens the respect of neighbors. Sub-section numbers vary by edition; confirm.
The script says plainly that 'ask' is the path's framing, not the handbook's wording.
'A method named after him': the Socratic method. Confirm phrasing.
